To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

one coreceptor protein, SERK3, contributes to the specific binding and activation of different ligand-bound receptor kinases, BRI1 and HAESA, and that the receptor kinase domain is responsible for their signaling specificity.

the SERK-family core receptor kinase contributes to the activation of plant receptor kinases by providing a second, constitutively formed binding interface and by stabilizing the ligand-receptor complex.
one coreceptor protein is able to contribute to the sensing and activation of two distinct receptors, which are involved in different signaling pathways.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a class of proteins that sense signals in plants, which are different than those used by the immune system of animals or the bacteria.
the activation mechanism of a plant membrane receptor by its coreceptor, which allows for the sensing of very different ligands and activation by distinct receptors.
how plants can sense and process different signals at their cell surface.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SERK3 acts as a coreceptor for two LRR-RK, which are activated by distinct ligands.
SERK-family core receptors can contribute to the activation of distinct receptor kinases by forming heterodimers with them, which are then activated by their respective ligands.
the coreceptor SERK3 is able to bind the ligand-bound receptor BRI1 with very similar binding affinities and kinetics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the SERK family of coreceptors is able to interact with different ligand-bound LRR-RK receptors, which are activated by the binding of the respective ligand.
the coreceptor kinase SERK is able to contribute to the activation of two different receptors with very distinct ligands.

a plant-specific coreceptor kinase is required for the activation of a family of plant membrane receptor proteins that are involved in sensing different types of ligands and in regulating plant growth and organ development.
The main takeaway from our work is that
one coreceptor protein is able to bind and activate receptors that sense very different signals.
one coreceptor protein, SERK, can be shared between different receptors, and that it can contribute to the binding of two different ligand molecules and the activation of two different receptors.
a single coreceptor protein can bind to two different ligand-bound receptor kinases, and thereby contribute to their activation.
